Customer: upload 14 days of anonymized traffic logs to shared S3 by 2026-03-30
Schedule microbench run and follow-up sync for week of 2026-04-06
action_items: Lena Park - Send benchmark template + measurement playbook (due 2026-03-26)
Marco Diaz - Run Redwood hosted microbench with Apex sample set (due 2026-04-02)
Ravi Shah - Provide anonymized traffic traces and typical prompt set (due 2026-03-30)
Carlos Mendes - Confirm network path/VPC requirements for private pilot (due 2026-04-01)
header: Date: 2026-03-25 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 min | Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Ravi Shah (ApexMetrics CTO), Emily Wong (ApexMetrics ML Eng), Carlos Mendes (ApexMetrics Infra)
summary: SE-led POC scoping focused on defining latency vs throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing and a 4-week benchmark/measurement plan. Customer wants clear acceptance criteria for both cold and warmed cache paths, sample size and traffic shape for the pilot. Agreed Redwood will run an initial microbench and share template; customer to provide traffic traces and confirm infra constraints for private pilot.
topics: Introductions; current stack & constraints; TTFT vs TPOT definitions; target p95/p99 thresholds; workload sampling and payload variance; benchmark methodology (synthetic replay, live traces, cache priming); measurement tooling and metrics; responsibilities and timeline
transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we have about 50 minutes today, main goal to align acceptance criteria for the P O C and a measurement plan. Are we good on agenda?
[00:00:12] Ravi Shah: Yes, thanks Lena. Quick context — ApexMetrics is shipping an LLM-based insights assistant for analytics, typical prompt length 120-450 tokens, about 65% short queries, 25% medium, 10% long-ish. We currently call external hosted models but cost and tail latency are an issue.
[00:00:35] Marco Diaz: Cool, helpful. Emily, can you give a quick snapshot of current perf and what you care about?
[00:00:40] Emily Wong: Sure. In production our 95th percentile time-to-first-token sits around 600 to 800ms depending on load, p99 is 1.6 to 2.1s which is painful. Per-token time (TPOT) varies a lot — streaming costs spike with longer responses, we see 20–40ms/token on average but heavy tails on some requests.
[00:01:05] Marco Diaz: Thanks. So for clarity — when we say TTFT we mean time from request receive at service edge to first byte/token emitted by the model. TPOT we'll treat as mean/percentile time per token during generation, including any batching overhead.
[00:01:20] Ravi Shah: Yeah, that's our mental model too. Also want both cold start and warmed cache numbers — sometimes customers hit the cold path after deploys.
[00:01:30] Lena Park: Absolutely. For the POC acceptance we'll surface both typical warmed path and cold-path (cold KV cache / no prefix). We'll propose separate SLO buckets.
[00:01:40] [00:01:45] Marco Diaz: Proposal — baseline SLOs: TTFT p95 <= 250ms warmed, p99 <= 500ms warmed; cold path TTFT p95 <= 600ms, p99 <= 1.2s. For TPOT, propose p95 <= 15ms/token warmed, p99 <= 35ms/token warmed. These are starting points given the model family you mentioned (we'll confirm exact numbers when we know the model/quantization).
[00:02:10] Emily Wong: Those warmed numbers are ambitious versus our current numbers but would be great. How do you measure TPOT for streaming vs non-streaming clients? Our frontend uses streaming for incremental updates.
[00:02:23] Marco Diaz: Good question — measurement plan covers both. For streaming we measure token emission timestamps at the Redwood runtime and at the client edge; we report delta to show network vs server contribution. For non-streaming we measure end-to-end total latency and calculate average per-token by dividing generation time by token count, but we prefer token-level telemetry.
[00:02:45] Carlos Mendes: Network contribution is key — some of our EU customers will be routed through a transit network. We need to isolate service-side latency.
[00:02:52] Lena Park: We'll provide tracing guidance — distributed trace spans that'll let us split network, edge, and model inference time. We'll also supply a small instrumentation snippet for SDK.
[00:03:05] [00:03:12] Ravi Shah: Sampling — what's the recommended sample size to make p99 stable for our workload? We have a fair amount of tail variance.
[00:03:20] Marco Diaz: Statistically p99 is noisy; for reasonable confidence we'd collect on the order of 10k+ requests per SLO bucket. Practically for the POC we recommend 10k samples per profile (short/medium/long) ideally across a few traffic shapes including bursty and steady. If you can't supply live traffic, we can replay anonymized traces.
[00:03:44] Emily Wong: Ok. How about sequence length distribution we should use for the microbench?
[00:03:50] Marco Diaz: Use your real distribution: e.g., 65% short (<=128 tokens), 25% medium (129-512), 10% long (512-1024). Include top-k/top-p settings and typical prompt templates. Those affect KV cache sizes and attention kernel selection.
[00:04:10] Lena Park: Also call out cache warmup strategy — we recommend priming with your top 200 customer prompts for warmed path tests, and a true cold path where we wipe KV cache for cold-start SLOs.
[00:04:23] Ravi Shah: Makes sense. What about batching behavior? Our traffic is spiky — will Redwood batch aggressively and increase TTFT?
[00:04:30] Marco Diaz: Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching with policy knobs. For low-latency tiers we bias toward immediate dispatch with smaller batches; for cost-optimized tiers we tank up larger batches. For the POC we can lock a policy so the microbench mimics your production dispatch (we'll capture cfg). We'll also measure tail under constrained capacity to validate graceful degradation.
[00:04:54] Emily Wong: We have a requirement: p95 TTFT must be under 300ms for 80% of user-facing queries during peak; otherwise we need to consider dedicated capacity. Can that be captured in the SLO definition?
[00:05:04] Lena Park: Yes, that's an acceptance rule we can express as a weighted SLO. During the benchmark we'll measure weighted percentile where traffic classes are weighted by your user-facing importance. We'll include that in the acceptance criteria doc.
[00:05:18] [00:05:25] Marco Diaz: Measurement tooling — Redwood will run two parallel experiments: 1) hosted microbench on Redwood hosted with your sample set to get baseline and kernel/quantization suggestions, 2) replay of your anonymized 14-day trace in a scale test to validate p95/p99 under realistic burstiness. We'll capture system metrics (GPU util, memory, queue length), per-request timings (edge, routing, model, stream) and token throughput.
[00:05:52] Carlos Mendes: For the private deployment we care about KMS/HSM integration and network egress. How do you simulate our on-prem path?
[00:06:00] Marco Diaz: For private pilots we run the same benchmarks inside a dedicated VPC with your network egress rules and attach an HSM stub for KMS latencies. It won't be the full HSM but we capture the added RTT. We'll note any differences in the measurement report.
[00:06:15] Ravi Shah: Timeline? We need results to decide on Dedicated vs Hosted by mid-April.
[00:06:20] Lena Park: Proposed timeline: week 0 (this week) — agree SLOs and collect traces; week 1 — Redwood shares benchmark template and runs microbench; week 2 — full replay tests and private VPC smoke; week 3 — analysis and SLO report; week 4 — acceptance review and decision. So about a four-week pilot.
[00:06:41] Marco Diaz: We'll also include a risk register — things like model mismatch, outlier payloads, and network chokepoints. If initial microbench fails warmed SLOs we can propose mitigations: model quantization, different kernel selection, or reserved concurrency (Dedicated).
[00:06:58] Emily Wong: For acceptance criteria language, can we have both absolute thresholds and a degradation policy? Example: absolute p95 TTFT warmed <= 300ms; if not met, allow 10% of requests to exceed up to 500ms but we want a remediation plan.
[00:07:12] Lena Park: Yes, we'll draft an acceptance matrix with hard gates and flexible gates. Hard gate: p95 warmed <= 350ms; Soft gate: weighted p95 across critical routes <= 300ms with remediation steps if soft gate missed. We'll circulate the matrix.
[00:07:25] [00:07:30] Marco Diaz: On instrumentation: please include SDK logs for token timestamps and a sampling of raw payloads. We'll hash identifiers for privacy. For the replay harness, we prefer an S3 bucket with compressed ndjson where each record contains prompt, expected token count, and simulated client RTT.
[00:07:52] Ravi Shah: We'll redact PII and send a sample 48-hour trace first. Good to hear about hash.
[00:07:58] Carlos Mendes: Security review — we will need SOC 2 docs and encryption at rest details before private deployment.
[00:08:05] Lena Park: We'll attach Redwood's compliance packet; Marco will follow up with the security docs link.
[00:08:12] [00:08:15] Emily Wong: One nit — when you run TPOT p99 numbers, do you include tokenization time? Our frontend tokenizes client-side, server-side tokenization adds some overhead.
[00:08:24] Marco Diaz: We'll instrument both. Our default TPOT excludes client-side tokenization unless you ask us to measure full end-to-end. We'll provide both reports.
[00:08:33] Lena Park: Recap of acceptance criteria items we agreed to capture: warmed TTFT p95/p99, cold TTFT p95/p99, TPOT p95/p99, weighted SLOs for user-facing routes, sample size per bucket, and a remediation plan.
[00:08:48] [00:09:00] Marco Diaz: Quick example numbers we'll put in the draft SLO doc (these are placeholders): WARMED TTFT p95 250ms / p99 480ms; COLD TTFT p95 600ms / p99 1.2s; TPOT warmed p95 15ms / p99 35ms. We'll refine once we know which exact model you want to serve (7B vs 13B vs 70B or an Open model).
[00:09:24] Emily Wong: For the microbench, will you test quantized variants? We recently evaluated 4-bit quantization.
[00:09:30] Marco Diaz: Yes, microbench will include float16 and recommended quant profiles; we'll surface perf vs quality tradeoffs. Redwood Optimize can propose quantization + batching config to hit cost/latency targets.
[00:09:42] Ravi Shah: How will you present results? CSV, dashboards?
[00:09:45] Lena Park: We'll deliver a measurement report (PDF) + CSV exports of raw latencies + a short walkthrough meeting. Also a perf dashboard link for interactive filtering.
[00:09:56] Carlos Mendes: If we decide Dedicated, what's the minimum commit? Do we have to wait until after the POC?
[00:10:02] Lena Park: We can discuss Dedicated commercial terms in parallel; usually committed monthly GPU pools are negotiated after pilot shows needed capacity. We can provide estimates earlier based on microbench.
[00:10:12] [00:10:18] Marco Diaz: A few practical notes for the measurement plan: 1) include a synthetic latency floor to account for network; 2) label requests by route and use-case so we can do weighted percentiles; 3) capture kernel-level metrics (e.g., attention kernel time) if you can provide access for deep dive.
[00:10:36] Emily Wong: We'll try to provide kernel-level logs for a short window.
[00:10:40] Ravi Shah: Ok, that's helpful. One more question: during high load, what's your fallback story? If Redwood can't meet SLOs, do you throttle, degrade quality, or route to a cheaper model?
[00:10:50] Marco Diaz: Redwood supports graceful fallbacks: routing to a cheaper quantized variant, shedding non-critical requests, or auto-scaling reserved capacity. We will include policy suggestions tailored to your SLA appetite.
[00:11:05] Lena Park: Great. Let's summarize next steps and owners. Marco will run microbench on Redwood hosted and share results; I'll send benchmark template and SLO matrix; Ravi/Emily/Carlos will provide traces and infra notes. Target follow-up sync after first microbench week of 2026-04-06.
[00:11:25] [00:11:30] Ravi Shah: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:33] Lena Park: Thanks all — we'll circulate notes and action items.
[00:11:36] [End of captured excerpt — remainder of the 52-minute call contains Q&A on specific prompt templates, a short demo of Redwood Console latency graphs (audio glitch), and scheduling confirmation.]
